# Green Sea Ocean Circulation

This is the working ocean model accompanying [[Taelgar Climatic Model]] and [[Trading in the Green Sea]]. It covers the [[Green Sea]], the [[Western Gulf]], and their exchange with the [[Outer Ocean]]. It establishes a regional pattern for temperature, marine productivity, and navigation; individual channels, current speeds, and underwater terrain remain open to development.

%% Speculative ideas generated by AI at user request; not canon. %%

## Whole-sea overview

**Cold water enters in the northeast, warm water enters in the southeast, and their branches feed a shared eastward outflow offshore between Ursk and Irrla.** The northern coastal current is relatively narrow and fast, especially under the summer easterlies. The offshore outflow is broader, and its surface flow slows substantially where those winds oppose it. Water continues returning east through a combination of surface and deeper routes.

## The three main branches

### Cold northern inflow

A branch of cold Outer Ocean water enters through the northern Eastern Isles and moves west along the northern margin of the Green Sea, past [[Ursk]] toward the northwestern basin. It occupies the upper ocean, with cooler water also extending beneath the seasonally warmed surface. Its influence changes as it mixes and exchanges heat along the route.

The main westward flow stays fairly close to shore. Summer easterlies reinforce it and make its speed especially useful to westbound ships. Near Skaerhem, islands, banks, and headlands divide and redirect the current: fast passages, quieter water, eddies, and offshore branches can coexist within the overall westward pattern. Their exact locations need local mapping. A portion of the northern water turns offshore to feed the confluence rather than continuing into the Western Gulf.

### Warm southern inflow

Warm upper-ocean water enters through gaps in the southern island chain and spreads west through the southern Green Sea. A branch turns north through the western basin, west of [[Irrla]], carrying warmth toward Cymea and the confluence. The coast and the Maritime Trade Peninsula divide this broad circulation into local branches; no single continuous coastal stream is required.

Southern spring and summer easterlies can reinforce the westward surface flow. Winter calms weaken wind assistance without shutting off all ocean exchange. The warm inflow maintains a southern and western heat reservoir, while its temperature is progressively modified by local weather and mixing.

### Shared offshore outflow

The branches approach one another off northern Cymea, toward the western end of the corridor between Ursk and Irrla. Their water moves east along a broad **ocean front**, a boundary between water masses with different temperature and salinity. Mixing continues downstream: the outflow contains warmer and cooler bands and eddies, rather than becoming uniformly lukewarm at one junction.

The main return crosses the open water north of Irrla and leaves through several eastern passages. Some flow occurs beneath the moving islands. The entrance and exit arrows identify regional exchange sectors, not particular navigable gaps or a requirement that the water follows one narrow route.

> [!tip] Why the outflow can continue when surface winds oppose it
> Wind acts most directly on the upper water. The broader circulation also responds to differences in sea level and density, shaped by the two inflows, heating, cooling, and basin geometry. Summer easterlies can slow the offshore surface current considerably while deeper or more widely distributed eastward flow continues. Over time, total inflow and outflow must balance, allowing for rivers, evaporation, and precipitation; the basin cannot simply accumulate water throughout the summer.

This requires adequate eastern outlet capacity and a suitable pressure pattern. The circulation is a physically motivated working hypothesis, not a numerical solution. Mixing itself does not supply the force that drives the outflow.

### Outer Ocean setting

The working external picture has a cold southward current approaching from the north and a warm northward current approaching from the south. They supply the northern and southern entrances and interact farther offshore, where the Green Sea's shared outflow rejoins them. Their meeting latitude, relative strength, and onward route remain flexible. This establishes regional water sources without assigning a complete global ocean circulation.

## Temperatures and seasonal changes

Water temperature reflects imported heat, sunlight, heat lost to the atmosphere, and mixing between depths. Winter cooling supplies additional cold northern water; southern inflow and summer sunshine add heat. Mixing redistributes that heat rather than creating an inexhaustible cold source. Temperature and salinity together determine which water can lie above or beneath another layer.

The northern coastal current can stay cool while sheltered bays warm considerably in summer. Well-mixed Skaer banks should warm less rapidly than a thin, sheltered surface layer. The shallow Western Gulf can have a substantial seasonal temperature range, interrupted by cooler patches along its upwelling coasts. The outflow's temperature depends on the proportions and histories of both inflows. No temperature ranges or extensive sea-ice cover are assigned here.

| Season | Main sea circulation and temperature | Western Gulf and navigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Winter | Northern westerlies generally assist offshore eastward surface flow and oppose or weaken the westward coastal branch. Cold-water supply continues beneath local surface variations; cooling and storms mix the northern upper ocean. Southern exchange persists during the maritime calms. | The gulf cools and loses some summer layering. Its sheltered character remains; cooling and occasional mixing do not require frequent severe storms. Northern voyages face winter weather and local harbor limitations. |
| Spring | Offshore eastward flow and returning light favor the spring sailing and bloom seasons. Northern cold water delays warming; southern easterlies begin assisting westward travel from Medju. The warm western branch supports northward progress offshore west of Irrla. | River inputs and increasing sunlight support coastal growth. Tollen ships can seek the offshore outflow, then cross the coastal current to reach Ursk. Selected port access by early to mid-May remains a trading-model requirement. |
| Summer | Northern E–NE winds strengthen the fast westward coastal current. Offshore surface outflow slows markedly where winds oppose it; the broader eastward return continues at depth or across a wider area. Warm surface layers develop where mixing is weak. Local westerlies nearer Irrla can leave parts of the outflow less opposed. | Western Cymea has favorable winds for localized upwelling. The northern return presents a choice between coastal speed and offshore sea room. Surface flow need not change everywhere on the same date. |
| Autumn | Returning westerlies favor offshore eastward voyages and weaken the coastal current's wind assistance. Cooling and storms erode summer layering. Westward coastal flow can persist through wind changes, creating rougher conditions when waves oppose it. | Autumn eastbound departures connect Ursk to selected island itineraries. A late coastal return requires weather judgment; the summer speed advantage does not establish a dependable extension after the wind reversal. |

> [!tip] Why summer winds strengthen the northern coastal current
> Along a south-facing Northern Hemisphere coast, winds blowing toward the west favor net surface-layer transport toward shore. Coastal accumulation and the resulting pressure slope can reinforce a westward current. This **downwelling-favorable** tendency is compatible with a cold current arriving from elsewhere; it does not imply that the water must be warm or that this coast is undergoing summer upwelling.

The wind response does not prescribe the current's full seasonal transport. A narrow current can become faster without carrying enough additional cold water to transform the whole basin. Numerical speeds, the width of the fast coastal core, and the timing of its seasonal changes remain unassigned.

## The Western Gulf

The Western Gulf exchanges water with the larger sea through the [[Straits of Cymea]]. It is not the terminus of the full fast northern current. Its circulation is smaller in scale: river plumes, seasonal winds, local coastal branches, and exchange through the straits redistribute water within a mostly shallow and sheltered basin.

Fresh river water spreads and mixes near the surface, while compensating marine inflow replenishes the gulf. If river input and rainfall exceed evaporation, a plausible average arrangement is surface export through the straits with saltier inflow beneath it. Winds and tides can temporarily reverse local flow. The freshwater budget and strait depths have not been established, so this layered exchange remains a candidate rather than an assigned permanent current.

%% Unassigned Gulf mechanism: the preceding surface-export/deeper-inflow arrangement is a proposed default for a net freshwater-receiving gulf. Neither the annual freshwater balance nor a sufficiently deep strait channel has been demonstrated. The map therefore shows two-way exchange without fixed vertical ordering or a permanent gulf-wide gyre. %%

Along western Cymea, the southward component of the summer winds can drive water away from west-facing shores. Cooler water from below replaces it, supplying nutrients where the local seabed and layering permit. The opposite side of the gulf can experience onshore transport under the same broad wind regime. The gulf therefore need not respond uniformly to a monsoon wind.

Rare deep canyons provide local complexity within the shallow sea. Their connections to the straits and surrounding shelf are unassigned; this model does not assume that abyssal Outer Ocean water can flow freely into them. The exact channels, shoals, and seasonal coastal currents can be developed around future locations without changing the basin model.

## Marine productivity

The name of the Green Sea reflects rich phytoplankton in its western waters. The model supports that abundance through several ordinary mechanisms: river nutrients, winter mixing, nutrient recycling in shallow water, mixing around banks and passages, and localized seasonal upwelling. Nutrients must reach the sunlit layer to support plant growth; cold water alone does not guarantee rich fisheries.

| Region | Main productivity pattern |
| --- | --- |
| **Skaerhem and the northwestern sea** | Proposed shallow banks and passage margins maintain productive patches through mixing and exchange with deeper water. Winter replenishment supports spring blooms; continued local mixing extends productivity into summer. Banks provide habitat for cod-like fisheries, while fronts and bank edges can concentrate prey for whales. Strong currents need places that retain or concentrate life as well as transport it. |
| **Western Gulf, especially western Cymea** | Rivers and shallow-water recycling support ordinary coastal fisheries. Localized summer upwelling along western Cymea can make the eastern gulf especially productive. River mouths and waters near Tollen remain productive enough to support its recorded inshore fishing fleet. The whole gulf need not be equally fertile. |
| **Urskan coast** | Ordinary coastal and river fisheries, with a spring bloom and local productive pockets. Fewer extensive banks, summer layering, and downwelling-favorable winds can limit sustained summer nutrient supply compared with Skaerhem. Ursk's cultural priorities remain a separate influence on its limited maritime emphasis. |
| **Central basin and shared outflow** | Clearer, less productive deep water can coexist with rich fronts, eddies, and island margins. The confluence creates opportunities for prey concentration, but mixing two currents does not automatically make the entire outflow fertile. |
| **Southern coast and Eastern Isles** | Localized productive shelves and passages. Summer westward winds can favor upwelling along appropriately oriented south-coast shores; island mixing depends on channel shape and depth. The remaining distribution is deliberately open. |

%% Source tension retained: [[Green Sea]] broadly attributes western productivity to monsoon-driven upwelling. This model narrows that explanation to favorable coast orientations and adds river inputs and mixing. The northern summer coastal current is downwelling-favorable; its fertility cannot be explained by generic summer upwelling. The reference note has not been rewritten here. %%

### Optional magical contribution

One Western Gulf canyon could contain an inflow from the [[Elemental Plane of Water]]. The existing [[Western Gulf]] account already records [[Ishara Venn]]'s unconfirmed claim of planar connections in its deep canyons. This remains an optional adoption of that rumor, not an established portal or a necessary part of the basin circulation.

The proposed ecological role is limited: an inflow drives persistent upward mixing of nutrient-bearing seawater, sustaining an unusually reliable feeding ground when ordinary seasonal upwelling weakens. Its depth, direction, and surrounding terrain must allow that influence to reach sunlit water; simply adding water far below the surface would not suffice. Its extra volume leaves through ordinary gulf exchange. No canyon location, flow rate, or basin-wide climatic effect is assigned, and no portal is marked on the map.

## Seamanship and trading choices

The fast coastal branch makes northwestern navigation valuable and difficult. The same current that helps a ship travel west can carry it rapidly toward a shoal, divide at an island, or leave a vessel in an unexpected eddy. Local knowledge includes when to enter the current, which passages to avoid, and where to stand offshore. These conditions support exceptional Skaer seamanship without making long-distance merchant trade central to Skaer society.

Tollish captains can use the summer coastal current for speed or take an offshore route with more sea room and less current assistance. They can also leave the coastal branch before its hardest reaches. The faster choice may permit a later departure within the summer window, but an autumn wind reversal raises its risks. The direct voyage still requires provisioning and endurance; no chain of safe Skaer stopovers is assumed. [[Trading in the Green Sea]] develops the commercial consequences and route calendar.

## Parameters left open

- Current speeds, widths, transport volumes, salinities, temperatures, and the vertical division of eastern exchange.
- The exact confluence position, seasonal movement, and degree of summer weakening of the offshore surface flow.
- Shelf edges, Skaer banks, navigable channels, tidal strength, and the local divisions of the coastal current. Map arrows cannot establish safe passages.
- The Western Gulf's freshwater balance, vertical exchange through the straits, canyon connections, and seasonal coastal circulation.
- The detailed strength and onward route of the Outer Ocean's warm and cold currents.
- Local sea ice, harbor opening dates, and the reach of any port magic. The cold inflow must remain compatible with the trading model's spring access requirement.
- Whether to adopt a single planar inflow, and what exceptional local feature it would explain.

## Physical comparisons and references

These sources support mechanisms and analogues, not calculated Taelgar conditions.

- [JMA: Oyashio](https://www.data.jma.go.jp/kaiyou/data/db/hakodate/knowledge/oyashio.html): a cold northern water source, fronts, seasonal reach, and substantial transport without exceptionally fast surface flow.
- [Yasuda et al., 1996: North Pacific Intermediate Water](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/phoc/26/4/1520-0485_1996_026_0448_damonp_2_0_co_2.xml): northern and southern water masses mixing while moving east through a frontal region.
- [NOAA: what drives currents](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/current.html) and [NASA: ocean topography](https://sealevel.jpl.nasa.gov/news/1126/dynamic-ocean-topography-with-current-arrows/): winds, density, sea-level differences, and rotation.
- [Keafer et al., 2005: coastal transport in the Gulf of Maine](https://www.whoi.edu/fileserver.do?id=35329&p=28251&pt=2): downwelling-favorable winds can strengthen and confine coastal transport.
- [NOAA: winter mixing](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/science-blog/winter-sets-oceans-clocks) and [coastal upwelling](https://www.psl.noaa.gov/news/2021/060821.html): seasonal nutrient replenishment and the importance of coastal orientation.
- [NOAA: Georges Bank](https://www.integratedecosystemassessment.noaa.gov/regions/northeast/georges-bank): productive shallow banks supporting cod, haddock, and whale feeding grounds.
- [NOAA: Northeast currents](https://www.integratedecosystemassessment.noaa.gov/regions/northeast/northeast-currents): shallow and deeper northern water sources; cold water is not necessarily richer in nutrients than warmer water.
- [WHOI: Where the whales are](https://www.whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/multimedia/where-the-whales-are/): fronts can concentrate prey into feeding patches.
- [NOAA: sea-state forecasting](https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/faq/sea_state_forecasting.shtml): waves opposing currents become steeper.
